name: Facemoji Keyboard
platform: Android (com.simejikeyboard; Lite: com.facemoji.lite) and iOS (App Store id1103138272)
vendor: Originally Baidu (built on the Simeji Japanese IME lineage, com.adamrocker.android.input.simeji); currently operated by Ekatox
evidence_quality: LOW-TO-MEDIUM. Closed source; no APK teardown, SDK docs, or theme-format specification is publicly available. No third-party technical teardown of Facemoji's theme packaging was found despite targeted searching. Findings below are assembled from the vendor's own marketing/help pages, app-store listings, hands-on feature reviews, and — where explicitly flagged — inference from the well-documented behavior of sibling commercial theme keyboards (Simeji/Baidu skins, Tappa's published KBThemes.json schema, Samsung IME 9-patch theming). Every inferred field is marked [uncertain].
rendering_approach:
[uncertain] Best evidence points to a **hybrid**: a whole-image background pasted behind a key layer, plus per-key overlay states drawn on top. Three observable behaviors force this reading. (1) Users supply an arbitrary photo from their gallery as a single keyboard-wide wallpaper, which only works as a whole-image paste — you cannot slice a user's photo into per-key art. (2) The DIY editor exposes independent **key opacity** and **brightness** controls, which only make sense if the key layer is a separate, alpha-composited layer over that background rather than baked into it. (3) 'Button style' / key-design is selectable independently of the background, implying key art is its own swappable layer.

So the model is almost certainly: background raster → optional dim/brightness scrim → per-key drawable (a shape or 9-patch, tinted/alpha-adjusted per user settings, with distinct normal/pressed states) → label glyph → transient tap-effect particle layer above everything.

What this is NOT: there is no evidence of genuine per-key *selector-based* theming in the FlorisBoard/CSS sense. Keys appear to be styled uniformly by role (normal vs functional vs enter/space) rather than individually addressable by key code. Marketing language reinforces the whole-keyboard framing — the pitch is that a theme 'can completely change the entire keyboard instead of having to tweak each element,' i.e. the product deliberately sells the opposite of per-key granularity. Curated store themes are plausibly richer (per-role art assets authored by designers) than DIY themes (background + uniform key treatment). [uncertain: all of the above is inferred; no decompiled evidence obtained]
selector_and_state_model:
[uncertain] No rule syntax exists to document — this is a closed, fixed-slot theming system, not a selector language. There is no stylesheet, no cascade, no specificity, and no user-authorable rule targeting. A theme fills a predetermined set of named slots defined by the app's own renderer.

Inferred targetable dimensions, from what the UI exposes and from sibling commercial formats:
- **Key state**: normal and pressed at minimum (pressed is universal in this app class; the tap-effect and key-preview popup confirm a pressed path exists). Disabled/focus/hover states are unlikely to be separately themeable.
- **Key role**: strong indirect evidence for role-based differentiation — normal alphanumeric keys, functional keys (shift/delete/symbols), the action/enter key (commonly accent-colored), and spacebar. Tappa's published commercial schema, a close analogue, splits colors into 'keys with borders' vs 'keys without borders' plus separate ABC-bar and toolbar colors, i.e. role-tiered rather than per-key.
- **Shift/caps state**: the shift key's own visual changes with state, but this is app-rendered behavior, not a theme-author-addressable selector. [uncertain]
- **Key code**: no evidence Facemoji lets a theme target one specific key by code. This is the sharpest capability gap versus FlorisBoard's `key[code=...]`.

User-facing 'selectors' are really global toggles: key opacity, brightness, text color, button style, font, sound, tap effect, swipe-trail effect. These apply keyboard-wide, not per key.
rendering_pipeline:
[uncertain] Android: almost certainly a **custom `View` with direct `Canvas`/`Drawable` drawing** inside an `InputMethodService`, not Jetpack Compose. Reasoning: the codebase descends from the Simeji IME lineage dating to 2008, long predating Compose; Compose inside an `InputMethodService` requires the `ViewTreeLifecycleOwner`/`SavedStateRegistryOwner` workaround and remains rare in shipping keyboards; and the app's heavy animated tap-effect/particle features are far cheaper on a hand-rolled canvas with a custom invalidation region than through recomposition. The classic AOSP-LatinIME-derived pattern — one custom `KeyboardView` that draws all keys in a single `onDraw`, with `invalidateKey(index)` to repaint only the touched key — is the likely design, and it makes per-keystroke cost low precisely because it avoids a full view-hierarchy pass.

iOS: a `UIInputViewController` keyboard extension, most likely UIKit with `UIView`/`CALayer` (possibly `CAEmitterLayer` for tap-effect particles) rather than SwiftUI, for the same memory-headroom reasons discussed under memory_performance_budget.

Platform blockers evidenced by user reports: reviewers describe 'delays or freezing while using the keyboard' and cases where 'the keyboard theme would automatically turn off and switch back to the regular keyboard by itself' — the latter is the classic signature of the OS killing an over-budget keyboard process, which is a rendering/memory-pipeline symptom rather than a theming-logic bug. [uncertain: no code-level confirmation of any of this]
compositing_scrim_model:
[uncertain] This is the one area where Facemoji's model is concretely better documented than FlorisBoard's, because the scrim is a **user-facing control rather than an implicit author choice**. Reviews of the DIY theme creator confirm it 'allow[s] users to fine-tune everything from key opacity and brightness to the swipe trail effect and key-press sounds' — so there are at least two independent compositing sliders.

Inferred stack, bottom to top:
1. Background image (user photo or store art), scaled to the keyboard frame.
2. A **brightness/dim scrim** over it — a black (or white) overlay whose alpha the user drives. This is the legibility mechanism: darken a busy photo until the key labels read.
3. Key layer, composited at a user-controlled **key opacity**, so keys range from fully solid to fully transparent (letting the photo show through the key caps).
4. Key labels/glyphs in a user-selectable text color, explicitly so users can 'make sure your keys pop against the background.'
5. Transient effect layers above everything: tap/press effects and the swipe/glide trail.

No concrete numeric values — no default scrim opacity percentage, no default key-alpha value, no blur radius — are published anywhere I could find. Blur is not mentioned in any source; gradient support is likewise unconfirmed. The important architectural takeaway for a per-key theming product is that Facemoji shifts the legibility burden onto the *user* via live sliders rather than onto the theme author or an automatic contrast checker. [uncertain: layer order and the existence of blur/gradient are inferred; no default values found]
asset_types:
[uncertain] Plain raster (PNG, near-certainly, with JPEG for user photos) dominates. For the key layer, **9-patch PNG (`.9.png`) is the strong inference** — it is the Android-native way to make one key-cap image stretch across variable key widths (a spacebar and a letter key share one asset), and sibling commercial keyboards demonstrably use exactly this: Samsung's IME ships `sip_key_bg_normal.9.png`, `sip_key_bg_option.9.png`, `sip_key_bg_pressed.9.png`. Facemoji's swappable 'button styles' map naturally onto swappable 9-patch sets.

Density bucketing is likely relevant for bundled/curated assets — the analogous Tappa commercial schema explicitly recommends shipping drawables at `mdpi`, `hdpi`, `xhdpi`, `xxhdpi` and `xxxhdpi`. Downloaded themes more plausibly ship a single high-density raster to keep payload small, letting Android scale.

Not evidenced: vector/SVG drawables, XML shape drawables, or Lottie for key art. Lottie or frame-sequence assets may back the tap-effect/particle animations, but no source confirms the format. User-supplied backgrounds are of course arbitrary JPEG/PNG from the gallery, decoded at runtime. Fonts ship as font files (50+ fonts are advertised). [uncertain: 9-patch usage, density bucketing, and animation asset format are all inferred from sibling products, not observed]
theme_package_manifest_format:
[uncertain] **No public specification exists.** Facemoji publishes no theme-authoring SDK, no format documentation, and no developer portal for theme submission — themes are produced in-house or via the in-app DIY editor, not by third-party developers, so the vendor has no reason to document the schema. Targeted searching for a Facemoji SDK, teardown, or theme spec returned nothing technical.

What can be reasoned about it:
- **Almost certainly a downloadable archive, not a plugin APK.** Themes are browsed and applied in-app from a store with 1,000-1,500+ themes, with a 'My Box' section managing installed themes. Installing 1,500 separate Android packages is untenable, and Play policy has progressively squeezed the legacy 'each theme is its own installable APK' model (the GO Keyboard era). A signed/opaque ZIP downloaded into app-private storage is the expected mechanism.
- **Likely a proprietary extension over ZIP.** The sibling Baidu input-method family uses a `.bds` skin file, described as a ZIP archive of theme resources with compression-method sensitivity. Facemoji sharing lineage with Simeji/Baidu makes a comparable vendor-specific container plausible, though the `.bds` evidence is for Baidu's Chinese IME rather than Facemoji itself. [uncertain — this is a family-resemblance inference, treat as weak]
- **Manifest almost certainly JSON** — the industry norm for this app class; Tappa's documented commercial equivalent is a single `KBThemes.json` holding an array of theme objects each keyed by an `order` integer, with ~19 color fields and ~6 drawable references.
- Expected fields: theme id, display name, version, author, preview image references, a color table, drawable filename references, font reference, sound reference, and effect id.

Treat the entire structure as unverified. A decompile of a downloaded theme payload from a real device is the only way to establish it.
token_count_tiering:
[uncertain] No published token count. The tiering, however, is clearly observable and is genuinely two-tier — this is the most transferable finding in this record.

**Simple tier (DIY / user-authored)**: a small fixed slot set the end user fills through a wizard — background image, key opacity, brightness, text color, button/key style, font, typing sound, tap effect, swipe-trail effect. Roughly 8-10 user-facing knobs. Reviews call this 'remarkably detailed' for a consumer tool, which calibrates the expectation: ~10 sliders reads as rich to users.

**Rich tier (curated/store themes)**: designer-authored packs with bespoke art per key role, matched emoji/sticker styling, custom sounds and effects. Token count unknown but necessarily larger.

For a numeric anchor, the closest published commercial schema (Tappa) exposes **19 colors + 6 drawables = 25 tokens**, covering toolbar items/active/background, brand main/secondary/misc, key text and background for bordered and borderless variants, status colors (neutral/good/warning/bad), keyboard background, cards, ABC bar, text colors, and a foreground accent. That is a reasonable order-of-magnitude estimate for Facemoji's internal table — a few dozen, not a few hundred, and nothing approaching FlorisBoard's ~90 elements × 24 properties combinatorial surface. [uncertain: Facemoji's own number is unknown; the 25 figure is from a different vendor's documented schema used as a proxy]
theme_versioning_forward_compat: [uncertain] Nothing published. Inferred from the delivery model rather than from any spec: because themes are served from a vendor-controlled store to a vendor-controlled client, Facemoji can version server-side — gate theme payloads on client app version and simply not serve a newer-schema theme to an older build. That sidesteps most forward-compat pressure and is the standard approach for closed marketplaces, so a schema-version field in the manifest is likely but its handling is invisible externally. Unknown/missing properties most plausibly fall back to built-in defaults rather than failing the theme load, since a partially-rendered theme is far better UX than a broken keyboard. The observable risk is the inverse: user reports of themes reverting to the default keyboard on their own could indicate load failures, though process-kill is the more likely explanation. Backward compat for the *user's own DIY themes* across app updates is a real concern for this app class and is not addressed in any documentation found. Entirely unverified.
color_extraction_dynamic_tinting:
[uncertain] Fully **pre-baked color values**, with no dynamic extraction — this is the clean architectural opposite of both Chrooma (per-app adaptive) and FlorisBoard (Material You wallpaper-derived). Nothing in Facemoji's feature set, marketing, or reviews mentions Material You, wallpaper-derived color, per-app adaptation, or automatic palette generation. Its entire proposition is the reverse: *expressive, art-driven, deliberately non-system-matching* themes — anime, K-pop, boba, avocado, Ironman, unicorn — where the point is that the keyboard looks like the theme, not like the OS.

One partial exception worth flagging: when a user builds a DIY theme from their own photo, the app *could* run something like Android's Palette API to pick a sensible default text/key color from that photo. Reviews describe users manually adjusting text color to make keys 'pop against the background,' which suggests manual choice is at least available and possibly the only path. Whether a smart default is seeded from extraction is unconfirmed. [uncertain]

Cross-platform consequence: because colors are pre-baked, the same color table is portable to iOS unchanged — an advantage of not depending on Material You.
contrast_enforcement_accessibility:
[uncertain] **No automated contrast validation is evidenced** — no mention of WCAG, APCA, contrast ratios, or automatic legibility checking anywhere in vendor material or reviews. Given the product's positioning (visual expressiveness over compliance) and its target demographic, automated enforcement is very unlikely.

What exists instead is a **manual, user-driven escape-hatch set**, which is genuinely the app's answer to legibility and is more end-user-empowering than FlorisBoard's author-only model:
- **Brightness slider** on the background — the primary tool for taming a busy photo.
- **Key opacity slider** — raising key opacity turns each key into a solid, legible plate over the art.
- **Manual text color** — reviews explicitly frame this as ensuring 'keys pop against the background.'
- **Key/button style selection**, which plausibly includes bordered vs borderless options, a border being the classic legibility escape hatch.

The burden therefore sits with the end user at DIY time, and with the in-house designer for curated themes. There is no evidence of a high-contrast mode, a system-accessibility-settings integration, a minimum-contrast clamp, or any refusal to apply an illegible combination. For a per-key theming product this is the cautionary finding: shipping opacity/brightness sliders is table stakes, but shipping them *without* any automatic floor means a meaningful share of user-made themes will be unreadable, and the app cannot detect it. [uncertain: absence of enforcement is inferred from silence across all sources, not confirmed]
background_geometry_adaptation:
[uncertain] Weakly documented and likely the app's softest engineering area. The mechanism is almost certainly **center-crop scaling of a single raster** to whatever frame the keyboard currently occupies, since users supply one arbitrary gallery photo and the app must make it work everywhere without asking anything further.

Specific pressures and what is known:
- **Portrait vs landscape**: aspect ratio changes drastically. The documented commercial analogue (Tappa) solves this by shipping **two separate wallpapers, portrait and landscape**, which strongly suggests one-image-crops-everywhere is visibly unsatisfying and that curated Facemoji themes may likewise ship per-orientation art. A DIY theme from a single user photo has no such luxury and must crop. [uncertain]
- **Variable keyboard height**: Facemoji offers keyboard resizing, so the background must reflow; crop-to-fill handles this but shifts which part of the image is visible.
- **Floating / one-handed / split modes**: whether the background re-crops, letterboxes, or is suppressed in these modes is entirely undocumented.
- **Tablets / iPad**: Facemoji is used on iPad (reviews cover iPad keyboard customization), where the keyboard is far wider relative to height, making crop artifacts worst. No adaptation strategy is documented.

Contrast with FlorisBoard, which exposes an explicit `content-scale` property and gives floating/one-handed/extracted modes their own themeable elements, so geometry adaptation is a first-class declared behavior rather than an implicit crop. [uncertain: entire field is inference; no source describes Facemoji's scaling behavior]
layout_locale_independence:
[uncertain] Likely robust, essentially for free, because of the whole-image background model — a background raster is indifferent to how many keys sit on top of it, so number-row on/off, non-QWERTY layouts, RTL scripts, and split layouts cannot break the background art. Facemoji supports many languages and layouts, and themes are marketed as universally applicable across them, with no per-layout theme variants offered — itself evidence that themes are layout-agnostic.

The fragile part is the key layer. If key art is 9-patch (as inferred), it stretches cleanly to any key width and any key count, so layout changes are safe. If any curated theme instead uses fixed-size per-position art, that theme would distort on unusual layouts — unverifiable without a teardown. Role-based styling (functional vs normal vs action) survives layout changes because roles persist across layouts, whereas position-based styling would not.

RTL is a layout-mirroring concern; a symmetric background is unaffected, but an asymmetric background (art weighted to one side) will read differently mirrored, and nothing suggests the app compensates. [uncertain]
non_key_surface_coverage:
[uncertain] Broad in practice — for a marketplace keyboard this is a commercial necessity, since a theme that stops at the key grid looks obviously unfinished and won't sell. Directly evidenced or strongly implied surfaces:
- **Key-press effects layer** — tap effects and the swipe/glide trail are explicitly themeable and are marketed features, notable because these are *motion* surfaces most keyboards don't theme.
- **Emoji / sticker / GIF panels** — central to the product (6,000+ emoji, sticker packs, GIFs) and presented as visually integrated with the theme. Emoji *style* (iOS-style vs Android-style glyphs) is separately user-selectable, which is adjacent to theming.
- **Toolbar / top bar** — the analogous commercial schema devotes several tokens to toolbar items, toolbar active state, and toolbar background, so coverage here is near-certain.
- **Suggestion/prediction strip** — likewise near-certain; it sits directly above the keys and would break the look if unthemed.
- **Key-preview popup and long-press mini-keyboard** — implied by the pressed-state and effects machinery, but not directly evidenced. [uncertain]
- **Settings/clipboard sheets and system nav bar color** — no evidence either way. Chrooma explicitly themes the navbar; Facemoji is silent. [uncertain]

Reviewers note 'the way themes and sticker packs are arranged makes it look rather bulky,' confirming themes and sticker content are bundled concerns in the UI. Overall, coverage is likely wide but shallow-and-fixed (a set number of themeable regions) versus FlorisBoard's ~90 individually addressable named elements.
sound_haptic_theming:
**Themed and swappable — and this is a genuine differentiator over open-source engines.** Multiple independent sources confirm typing sounds are part of the theme/customization surface: users can 'personalize tapping effects and sounds,' 'sound effects can be selected to make typing more engaging,' and the DIY creator tunes 'the swipe trail effect and key-press sounds' alongside visual properties. So a theme is an audio-visual bundle, not just a skin — a curated K-pop or anime theme can ship its own key-press sound.

Platform APIs are not documented. [uncertain] On Android, `SoundPool` is the expected mechanism for short, low-latency, frequently-repeated key sounds (with `AudioManager` for stream/volume and respect for the system keypress-sound setting); on iOS, `AudioServicesPlaySystemSound` or `AVAudioPlayer`, noting that a keyboard extension without Full Access is restricted in what it can play.

Haptics: not mentioned as *themeable* in any source. Vibration-on-keypress almost certainly exists as a global user preference (universal in this app class) but appears to be a setting rather than a theme-carried property. [uncertain]

Takeaway for a theming product: sound-as-part-of-theme is cheap to implement, highly visible to users, and something FlorisBoard's Snygg explicitly cannot do.
platform_apis_frameworks:
[uncertain] **Android**: `InputMethodService` as the IME host; a custom `View` subclass with `Canvas`/`Drawable` rendering for the key grid (see rendering_pipeline); `NinePatchDrawable` for stretchable key art and `BitmapFactory` for background decode; `ColorFilter`/`PorterDuff` or alpha modulation for the opacity and brightness sliders; `SoundPool`/`AudioManager` for themed key sounds; likely a `BroadcastReceiver`-free, purely in-app theme switch. No evidence of Jetpack Compose, and no evidence of Material You / `DynamicColors`.

**iOS**: a `UIInputViewController`-based keyboard extension paired with a containing app; UIKit `UIView`/`CALayer` rendering (possibly `CAEmitterLayer` for tap-effect particles); an **App Group shared container** to move downloaded themes from the container app to the extension — this is the only supported mechanism on iOS and is effectively forced by the architecture. `RequestsOpenAccess` (Full Access) is required, which is directly confirmed by the vendor.

Both platforms additionally need network + storage for the theme store, and the app is documented at 34.1 MB installed (Android), with a Lite build under 8 MB. Nothing here is confirmed at code level. [uncertain]
delivery_installation_pipeline:
Partly confirmed, partly inferred. **Confirmed**: themes are browsed and downloaded from an in-app store (1,000-1,500+ themes, new ones weekly), managed in a 'My Box' section, and applied from within the app. Users also create DIY themes locally from a gallery photo. Themes are explicitly shareable — 'share the custom keyboard so friends can use the same design' — implying an exportable/serializable theme representation and a server-side share/import path.

**iOS pipeline is the best-documented part, and it is confirmed by the vendor**: the user installs the container app, adds the keyboard via Settings → General → Keyboard → Keyboards → Add New Keyboard, and must enable **Allow Full Access**. Facemoji's own help material states that *'to preview or apply new themes, you need to ensure you have switched to Facemoji keyboard and enabled Allow Full Access.'* That sentence is the load-bearing fact: theme preview and application are gated on Full Access because the extension needs the App Group shared container (and network) to reach theme assets the container app downloaded. Assets therefore land in the shared App Group directory, not the extension's own sandbox.

**Android**: [uncertain] downloaded theme payloads almost certainly land in app-private internal storage under a per-theme directory, applied by switching the active theme id in preferences. No separate APK is installed per theme — the legacy plugin-APK model appears not to be used, and Play policy has made it unattractive. No signing or integrity scheme is documented.

Bundled-in-APK themes also exist: reviews note default themes 'pre-installed' alongside the downloadable catalog.
permission_store_policy_surface:
**iOS Full Access (`RequestsOpenAccess = YES`) is required and vendor-confirmed** — and specifically required *for theming*, not merely for prediction or sync. Facemoji's own material states iOS 'has some limitations on third-party keyboards, so Facemoji keyboard needs the permission of Allow Full Access to get full features,' and that previewing or applying new themes requires it. The vendor pairs this with a trust-reassurance line ('will not collect any personal information without user's permission'), which is itself evidence that Full Access is a known conversion obstacle for this product category. This is the single most important delivery constraint for any iOS theme marketplace: **downloadable themes are structurally incompatible with a no-Full-Access keyboard**, because without it the extension cannot reach network or the shared container.

Store-policy surface:
- Themes are inert data (images, colors, sounds, fonts), not executable code, so downloading them at runtime does not violate Apple's or Google's prohibitions on downloading executable code. This is the reason the ZIP/asset-bundle model is used rather than the legacy per-theme plugin APK. [uncertain: exact payload contents]
- Keyboards are a heightened-scrutiny category on both stores because they can observe all typed input; App Store review specifically probes Full Access justification, and Play requires data-safety disclosure.
- User-generated DIY themes built from gallery photos require photo-library access on both platforms and raise UGC-moderation questions if such themes are shared publicly. [uncertain: whether shared DIY themes are moderated]
- Android: no equivalent of Full Access; enabling the IME in system settings is sufficient.
memory_performance_budget:
This is the field where the closed-source evidence is most actionable, because the *constraint* is public even though Facemoji's mitigation is not.

**iOS is the binding constraint.** Keyboard extensions are limited to roughly **30-40 MB of dirty memory and ~77 MB total**, and exceeding it terminates the keyboard — the OS kills it and the system keyboard reappears. This ceiling is not vendor-specific; it is the documented reality every third-party iOS keyboard has faced since 2014. Two known aggravators apply directly to Facemoji: (a) **emoji rendering is a notorious memory spike** on iOS — a well-documented CoreText emoji retention issue caused memory to balloon when emoji were rendered on screen, and Facemoji is an emoji-first product with 6,000+ emoji, sticker packs and GIFs; (b) full-bleed background images decode to large uncompressed bitmaps (a naive full-resolution decode of a modern phone photo alone can exceed the entire dirty-memory budget).

User reports consistent with hitting this ceiling: complaints that 'the keyboard theme would automatically turn off and switch back to the regular keyboard by itself' and reports of delays/freezing. That revert-to-default signature is textbook extension termination.

**Mitigations are not documented** [uncertain], but the constraint mathematically forces some combination of: aggressive downsampling of background images to keyboard-frame pixel dimensions (never full-resolution decode), `inSampleSize`/`ImageIO` thumbnail decode paths, decoding to a lower-bit-depth or non-alpha config where possible, a small LRU bitmap cache with prompt eviction on theme switch, releasing assets on `didReceiveMemoryWarning`, and strictly capping how much of the emoji/sticker catalog is resident. Whether animation is permitted under this budget is unclear — animated themes are heavily memory- and CPU-intensive and would sit poorly inside 40 MB. [uncertain]

**Android is far more forgiving** — no comparable hard extension ceiling — which likely explains why the Android build is the feature-richer one. App install size is 34.1 MB with a sub-8 MB Lite variant, and users are advised to keep 100-500 MB free for cache; reviewers split between praising it as lightweight and calling the theme/sticker arrangement 'bulky.'
untrusted_theme_validation_security:
[uncertain] **Nothing published.** No source describes archive validation, decode limits, or malformed-manifest handling. The threat model is nonetheless real and worth stating, because it is the same one any theme marketplace inherits:
- **Zip-slip / path traversal** on unpacking a downloaded theme archive — the canonical defense is canonicalizing each entry path and verifying it stays under the theme's base directory (exactly what FlorisBoard's `FlorisAssetResolver` does). Whether Facemoji does this is unknown.
- **Decompression bombs / oversized images** — a hostile or merely careless PNG can blow the iOS 40 MB extension budget at decode time and kill the keyboard. A hard pixel-dimension cap before decode is the standard defense.
- **Malformed manifest** — should degrade to defaults rather than crash; no evidence either way.
- **Font files** — custom fonts (50+ advertised) are parsed by native text engines and are a historically rich attack surface.

Mitigating context: the catalog is **vendor-curated**, not open third-party submission. Themes come from Facemoji's own store and are in-house-produced, which substantially reduces exposure to genuinely hostile payloads compared with an open marketplace — the trust boundary is the vendor's server plus TLS, not arbitrary authors. If user-shared DIY themes propagate between users, that boundary weakens. This curation-instead-of-validation posture is common and is the pragmatic model, but it means the client-side hardening is unknown and possibly thin.
open_source_reference_availability:
**No source available.** Facemoji is fully closed source with no published theme-authoring SDK, no developer documentation portal, no theme-format specification, and no third-party technical teardown that I could locate despite targeted searching across GitHub, teardown writeups, and developer communities. There is no B2B/SDK offering for embedding the keyboard either — searches for one returned only consumer-app results. (An unrelated GitHub repo named `face-moji/face-moji` exists and is not this product.)

The only routes to its internals are: (1) decompiling the Android APK (`com.simejikeyboard`, ~34 MB; or the Lite build `com.facemoji.lite`) and inspecting `assets/`, `res/drawable-*/`, and the theme-download cache directory on a device with a theme applied; (2) intercepting theme-download traffic to capture a payload; (3) inspecting the iOS App Group container. Note the lineage — Simeji (`com.adamrocker.android.input.simeji`, Baidu Japan) — may make Simeji/Baidu skin documentation a useful proxy, and the Baidu input-method family's `.bds` skin container is the nearest documented relative. For an actually-documented commercial schema to study instead, Tappa publishes its Android keyboard theme format openly at https://developers.tappa.com/docs/android-keyboard-themes.
authoring_tooling_preview_generation:
**In-app DIY theme editor is confirmed and is a core marketed feature** — reachable via 'Customize' on the app home page, alongside 'Themes'. Reviews call the DIY creator 'remarkably detailed,' with controls spanning background selection (built-in library or gallery photo), key opacity, brightness, text color, button/key style, font, key-press sounds, tap effects and swipe-trail effects. Live preview is strongly implied on iOS — the vendor's own wording is that Full Access is needed 'to preview or apply new themes,' confirming a preview step exists as a distinct action. Themes are also **shareable between users**, which is unusual and implies an export/serialize path plus some hosted distribution.

No external/desktop authoring toolchain is published, consistent with themes being produced in-house or by end users rather than by third-party designers.

**Preview/thumbnail generation for the store**: not documented for Facemoji [uncertain], but the closest published commercial schema is instructive and likely representative — Tappa requires **three preview variants per theme**: a large preview *with* key borders, a large preview *without* key borders, and a small preview. That is a concrete, easily-overlooked requirement for anyone building a theme marketplace: the store card is not one image, and previews must be generated per border-mode because border mode is a user toggle that changes the theme's appearance. Facemoji's store, with 1,000+ themes browsed visually, necessarily has a comparable multi-image asset requirement.
cross_platform_token_parity:
[uncertain] Facemoji ships on **both iOS and Android** with what is presented as the same theme catalog and the same DIY feature set, so a meaningful degree of cross-platform token parity clearly exists in practice — a user picks 'the same theme' on either platform. This is materially helped by the color model being fully pre-baked rather than Material You-derived: static colors, raster backgrounds, and font/sound references all port unchanged.

Whether one literal theme *definition file* is consumed by both clients, or whether a shared source definition is built into two platform-specific payloads, is unknown. [uncertain]

Inherently platform-bound elements:
- **9-patch key art** is an Android-specific format with no iOS equivalent; iOS would use `UIImage.resizableImage(withCapInsets:)`, which is conceptually equivalent but a different asset encoding — so key-art assets likely diverge even when colors do not.
- **Emoji glyph rendering** differs by platform font (the app offers iOS-style vs Android-style emoji as a *setting*, itself an acknowledgment of this divergence).
- **Sound APIs** differ (`SoundPool` vs `AudioServices`/`AVAudioPlayer`), though the sound *asset* ports fine.
- **Delivery** diverges hard: App Group + Full Access on iOS versus ordinary app-private storage on Android.
- **Memory budget** diverges hard: iOS's ~40 MB ceiling may force lower-resolution or fewer assets on iOS for the identical theme.

Practical lesson: colors, fonts, sounds and background rasters port cleanly; stretchable key art, emoji, and the delivery/permission layer do not.
animation_budget:
**Flag as an open, weakly-documented question — but animation demonstrably exists.** Confirmed animated surfaces: tap/typing effects that 'appear when you press keys,' a swipe/glide **trail effect**, and 'Flow Option' and 'Effect Option' settings that 'add cool animations and visuals every time you type.' So motion is a first-class, marketed, theme-associated feature — a clear contrast with FlorisBoard, which has no animation support in its theme engine at all.

What is **not** documented anywhere: whether the *background* itself can be animated (Lottie/GIF/video) as opposed to only the effect overlays; the asset format for effects (Lottie vs sprite sheet vs particle system vs GIF); any frame-rate cap; and whether animation pauses when idle. The sibling Simeji product is described as supporting 'a photo, artwork, or even a **video** as the background,' which raises the possibility that Facemoji supports animated/video backgrounds too — but that is evidence about Simeji, not Facemoji, and should not be relied on. [uncertain]

The iOS ~40 MB extension budget is the hard constraint that any animated-background feature must live inside, and it makes video or high-resolution frame-sequence backgrounds expensive-to-implausible on that platform; effect overlays (short, small, GPU-composited particles) fit comfortably. A reasonable expectation is that effects animate on both platforms while animated backgrounds, if they exist, are Android-first or absent. Idle-pause behavior is unaddressed in every source, and is a battery-relevant question worth resolving empirically. [uncertain]
